tiger_m_tools: React, TypeScript, Tauri, PocketBase, Hostinger VPS
tiger_s_context: The Young Tiger distributes farming machinery and generators in Lomé: three shops, one warehouse and around ten distributors. When I started working with them in February 2026, everything was handled by hand. I first set up their PCs and a first management tool on Google Sheets.
tiger_s_problem: With three shops, a warehouse and distributors taking stock to resell, the spreadsheet could no longer keep up. The owner wanted to know at any moment what sells, where the stock is and who owes what, without being on site.
tiger_s_solution:
The spreadsheet quickly hit its limits. So I scoped, built and deployed a real management app myself:

  • Three roles, three interfaces: the seller cashes in and prints the invoice, the manager runs all three shops, the owner follows everything from his phone.
  • Sales and credit: the amount received decides whether a sale is cash or credit, the debt opens on its own and is paid off instalment by instalment, with a receipt each time.
  • Inventory and warehouse: stock arrivals, transfers from the warehouse to the shops, low stock alerts, no way to sell more than what exists.
  • Distributors: stock held and debt of each distributor calculated live.
  • Documents: invoices, quotes, receipts and delivery notes in A5 duplicate, based on the template the client already used.
  • Go-live: VPS server, domain name, app installed on the shop PCs and on the owner's phone.
tiger_s_results:
• App in production since September 2026, used daily by the owner, 2 managers and 3 sellers
  • Three shops, a warehouse and around ten distributors connected in a single tool
  • More than 200 products in the catalogue
  • The owner tracks sales, stock and credit remotely
  • Four types of printed documents generated automatically
tiger_s_learned: The hardest part was not the code but understanding how this business really works: distributors, credit, sales paid in several instalments. I learned to break a big project into stages, get each one approved by the client and handle a real production launch.
erp_m_tools: Python, SQLite, Supabase, Google Apps Script
erp_s_context: Many shop owners in Lomé still track stock and invoices on paper or in a makeshift Excel file. Alpha ERP was built for them: a simple, affordable tool that keeps running when the internet drops.
erp_s_problem: Amirson Machine sells machines in Atakpamé while the owner lives in Lomé. He wanted to follow his business remotely. A first step, a read-only dashboard synced from V1, confirmed the need. But the owner wanted more than a view: a real connected app he could use from his phone.
erp_s_solution:
Alpha now comes in three tiers:

  • Google Sheets ERP (entry level): automated invoicing with Apps Script, one click invoices, sales and customer credit tracking.
  • Alpha ERP V1 (desktop software): a Windows app in Python with a local SQLite database. Inventory, sales, credit, PDF invoices (A4, A5, 80 mm receipt), daily cash closing and machine-bound licence key.
  • Alpha ERP V2 (web): two apps connected to the same Supabase database. The seller app, on the shop PC, opens straight on “New sale”. The owner app, installed on his phone, shows a dashboard with charts, exports invoices as PDF, sends them over WhatsApp and exports data to Excel.
erp_s_results:
• V2 installed at Amirson Machine in July 2026
  • The owner follows his sales from Lomé, in real time
  • Sales by unit or by the metre, three invoice formats
  • Adapted for Amirson Quincaillerie, with sales by the metre, the litre and the roll
erp_s_learned: Moving from V1 to V2 taught me when to start over. Rather than patching more than 10,000 lines of Python, I rebuilt the tool for the web while keeping the same data model, and the installation landed on time.
erp_g1: Alpha V2: sales screen (invoice, quote, distribution)
erp_g2: Alpha V2: inventory with thresholds and alerts
data_s_context:
ASSAFETO wanted, for the first time, a digital database of all its members across the country. No central register existed: depending on the region, data was scattered, incomplete or missing.

The database had to help manage members, improve internal communication and give the association a reliable reference file.
data_s_problem: How do you collect and clean more than 1,900 answers from all over Togo, typed by people not used to digital tools and shared through WhatsApp groups, and deliver a clean file sorted by region?
data_s_solution:
A three step process:

  • Collection: a structured Google Form (identity, region, entry and exit dates), shared in the association's regional WhatsApp groups.
  • Cleaning: removing duplicates (sometimes the same person four times), fixing typing errors, standardising formats with advanced Google Sheets formulas.
  • Validation: lists sent to each regional lead for review, then their corrections merged in.
data_s_results:
• 1,900+ answers collected, reduced to 1,400+ real members
  • The association's first centralised digital database
  • Data sorted by region for local management
  • A clean file usable from day one, plus one PDF per region
data_s_learned: The real difficulty in data cleaning is not technical, it is human: you have to anticipate the mistakes of hundreds of people without losing useful information. I also learned to explain things simply, gather feedback and deliver a reliable result from very raw data.

proj_barber_desc: Online booking, a flexible schedule and loyalty for a barbershop in Lomé. A no-account client app and a barber dashboard, built for the phone.
barber_s_context: In Lomé, booking a barber still happens over the phone or on WhatsApp. The barber answers between two cuts, forgets to write it down, and two clients show up at the same time. I wanted a tool for a single shop, not yet another marketplace: the app carries the shop's name and doubles as its marketing tool.
barber_s_problem: How do you let clients book on their own, with no account or password, while the barber stays in control of his schedule, and without two people ever getting the same slot?
barber_s_solution:
Two apps in one project:

  • The client app, installable on the phone: pick a service, see the slots that are really free, apply a promo code, then follow bookings, points and vouchers.
  • The barber dashboard, on computer and phone: requests arrive live, he accepts, declines or suggests another time, and each action prepares a ready-made WhatsApp message.
  • The phone number as a loyalty card: every way of writing it (“90 11 22 33”, “+228 90112233”…) is normalised so one client stays one client.
  • Points you can't game: they are credited when the barber marks the client as present, and a personal voucher is created automatically at the threshold.
  • Built-in marketing: promotions on the home screen, promo codes open to all or tied to one number, and a list of clients who haven't come back in six weeks.
barber_s_results:
• Two complete apps: 8 client screens, 12 barber screens
  • Passwordless yet secure: a secret token per phone, no direct table access
  • Every booking rechecked in the database (hours, overlaps, price, promo code) by PostgreSQL functions
  • Business logic covered by unit tests (Vitest)
  • A full demo mode that runs in the browser, with no server
barber_s_learned: The most interesting part wasn't the interface but the business rules: what is a free slot when there's a break, a pending request and an open proposal? Who can see what without an account? Writing those rules once, testing them, then having the database enforce them is what makes the tool reliable.

barber_g7: Barber: client card, points and history
proj_quin_desc: The hardware store edition of Alpha for Amirson Quincaillerie: a till that sells by the metre, the litre or the roll, stock you count the way you do on the shelf, and invoices ready for the shop stamp.
quin_m_status: Approved, goes live after the stock count
quin_s_context: After Alpha V2 went live at Amirson Machine, the family's second shop, Amirson Quincaillerie, wanted the same tool. But a hardware store doesn't sell like a machine shop: the same cable goes out by the metre or by the roll, paint by the litre or by the bucket, nails by the kilo or by the box. For now the owner runs the counter himself, and a seller may join him later.
quin_s_problem: How do you keep one accurate stock when an item sometimes leaves by the metre and sometimes by the roll, without turning every sale into a conversion exercise, and without losing a sale when the internet drops?
quin_s_solution:
I took the Alpha product and reworked the data model around units:

  • A base unit and packagings: stock is counted in the smallest unit sold, and each packaging has its own price. Selling 2 rolls removes 200 m, and stock reads in plain words: “3 rolls + 25 m”.
  • A till built for the counter: catalogue on the left, ticket on the right, and each item offers its selling options right away (by the metre, 100 m roll). Change due and the amount on credit are worked out automatically.
  • Sales calculated by the database: a PostgreSQL function records the sale, the profit and the stock movement in a single transaction. A sale made offline and sent once the network is back never creates a duplicate.
  • One app, two roles: the owner sees everything, the seller never sees purchase prices or profits. It isn't a hidden screen, the database itself refuses (RLS rules).
  • Deliveries and stock counts: a supplier delivery note raises the stock and updates the purchase price, and the stock count works the way you count on the shelf, in mixed units.
  • Direct printing: A4, A5, receipt or duplicate invoices straight from the browser, plus an Excel import of the catalogue for stock count day.
quin_s_results:
• Approved by the client, going live after the stock count
  • 44 automated database tests: units, permissions, credit, cancellations, offline sales
  • 10 screens: till, documents, credit, stock, dashboard, products, deliveries, team, activity log, exports
  • One app instead of the two used in the Amirson Machine version
  • A dark “Workshop” interface built for the counter, with a light theme for bright sunlight
quin_s_learned: The real topic wasn't the screen but the model: a quantity only means something with its unit. Picking a base unit and conversion factors, then letting the database do the maths, is what keeps the stock right whichever way you sell. I also learned not to assume anything about an online service: new Supabase projects no longer expose tables to the API by default, and it was a carefully read error message, not a hunch, that showed it.

proj_alb_desc: Point of sale, customer credit, inventory and stock counts for a wholesale grocery shop in Lomé. Built for the phone, it keeps selling when the power goes out.
alb_s_context:
ETS AL BARAKAT is a grocery shop that mostly sells wholesale: rice by the bag, oil by the carton, pasta by the box. The manager works with an assistant, takes cash, T-Money or Flooz, and gives credit to trusted customers.

Instead of an interview, I had her fill in an online questionnaire. Her answers shaped everything: her number one fear was losing control of what leaves the shop, her priority was making stock counts easy.
alb_s_problem: How do you give the manager control over stock and cash in front of her assistant, with no barcode scanner, and with power cuts that regularly switch off the internet box?
alb_s_solution:
Every questionnaire answer became a decision:

  • A till that does the maths: carton, box or tiered prices (“150 F from 3”), change due or balance on credit, split payments in cash and T-Money, receipt sent over WhatsApp.
  • Two roles, clear limits: the assistant sells but never sees the day's total or the stock value. Out of stock, credit limit exceeded, price changed or free item: she is blocked until the manager enters her code.
  • Credit like a notebook: each customer has an account, a limit, partial repayments and a one-tap WhatsApp reminder.
  • Stock under control: deliveries update the purchase price, losses, breakage and theft are logged with a reason, counts are done by the assistant and approved by the manager.
  • A blind end-of-day cash count: the assistant counts the drawer without seeing the expected amount, the manager then compares each payment method.
  • It sells even offline: sales stay on the device and are sent automatically when the network returns, never twice.
  • Invoices ready to go: cut-in-half duplicate or full A4, over several pages if needed, with the amount written in words.
alb_s_results:
• App delivered as v1.0, installed on the manager's computer and phone
  • Before go-live, a tester outside the project attacked the app: 19 issues found, all fixed and rechecked
  • Updates without reinstalling anything: the app shows “A new version is ready”
  • Free hosting, with the database woken up automatically every morning
alb_s_learned: Starting from the client's fear rather than a feature list changed everything: stock control became the thread of the whole app, from the unlock code to the blind cash count. And having someone else attack my work before delivery showed me 19 flaws I would not have found alone.
alb_g1: Manager home: day total, credit, alerts
alb_g3: Checkout: change due and split payment
alb_g4: Credit sale: the customer is recognised
alb_g5: Receipt ready to send on WhatsApp

antre_s_context:
After every outing with friends, the photos scatter: some on WhatsApp, some on Snapchat, most stay on people's phones. Three weeks later, nobody can find the beach photo or remember who was there. The group's memories had no home.

Before coding, I validated the idea: I pitched it to the group, then had them try an HTML prototype on their phones. They were in, so I started the real build.
antre_s_problem: How do you build a private place for a single group, pleasant enough that people want to come back, without letting just anyone in, and with zero budget?
antre_s_solution:
An installable web app, designed for the phone first:

  • Joining the group: a single-use invite code, then a 4-step sign-up that ends on a numbered member card under confetti.
  • Creating an outing in seconds: the date in one tap (“Today”, “Yesterday”, “Last Saturday”), known places suggested, attendees ticked by tapping their face.
  • One album per outing: cover, “who was there”, free emoji reactions and comments on every photo. Those who missed it still see everything, and the album downloads as a .zip or straight to the phone's gallery.
  • The feed and the bell: recent albums, a memory of the day drawn from older photos, and a bell that only lists what concerns you.
  • Real-time group chat: instant messages, “Marco is typing…”, who's online, reactions with a long press.
  • A real app without a store: installable on the home screen, push notifications even when closed (iPhone included), a clean offline page, light or dark theme.
antre_s_results:
• Live and used by my group of friends, on a 100% free stack (Vercel, Supabase, Cloudinary)
  • Code audited before opening up: guessable invite codes, one code creating several accounts, a member able to make himself admin, public sign-up left open. All fixed
  • Invite codes now 8 characters, valid for 7 days, with limited attempts, and access rules (RLS) on every table
  • Automatic wake-up every morning so the free database never falls asleep again
antre_s_learned: A cheap prototype kept me from building the wrong thing. Having fresh eyes review my code let me find the flaws before anyone else did. And emotional details matter as much as features: the member card did more for adoption than any setting.
antre_g1: The feed: latest outings and activity

proj_ytv_desc: Logo, brand guidelines, Google listings, social accounts, a 200+ product showcase website and motion videos: the whole online presence of a brand that had none, built to lead to a WhatsApp conversation.
ytv_m_role: Visual identity, strategy, website, social and videos
ytv_m_tools: Figma, Canva, CapCut, HTML/CSS/JS, Netlify, Meta Business Suite, WhatsApp Business, Google Business Profile
ytv_m_status: Website live and indexed on Google, 7 videos ready
ytv_s_context: When I started with The Young Tiger, the brand had no online presence at all: no logo, no brand guidelines, no Google listing, no social accounts, no website. A customer looking for a generator in Lomé simply couldn't find them. I built everything from scratch.
ytv_s_problem: How do you make a brand findable and make people want to get in touch, no prices shown, and customers browsing on 3G phones? The common thread: every touchpoint, Google, social and website, leads to a WhatsApp conversation with a seller.
ytv_s_solution:
Everything, from the brand to the videos:

  • Visual identity: the logo, the brand guidelines (white first, orange accents), posters and print material.
  • Google: created the Google Business listings for each shop, with the pin on the storefront, opening hours and a link to the website, then submitted the site to Search Console with a sitemap and business details Google can read.
  • Social: created the Facebook, Instagram and TikTok accounts, wrote the bios, connected everything in Meta Business Suite. WhatsApp Business set up with a greeting, an away message and quick replies, including one with the Maps link of each shop.
  • The showcase website: the tagline “When the power goes out, the tiger wakes up”, four use cases (home, shop, field, worksite), a 200+ product catalogue pulled from the management software, galleries for products shot from several angles, and a WhatsApp button with a pre-written message on every product.
  • Videos: I produce them myself, 7 so far. Motion videos built from animated text (“The tiger wakes up”, “Is your business stopping?”, “How much power for my home?”, “Power cut”), before / after videos edited with royalty-free footage (“Is your field wearing you out?”, “From paddy to white rice”) and a “New arrivals” video edited with real factory footage sent by the client. Every video ends on the same end screen, in 9:16 and 4:5.
  • Posts: an “Our shops” carousel, 31 cut-out product photos for the team's posters, ready-to-paste captions and a launch calendar of 10 posts.
ytv_s_results:
• A brand that started from zero and now exists everywhere: Google, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp Business and a website
  • The website shows up on Google for “The Young Tiger Lomé”, right under the shops' Maps listings, with both pages indexed
  • 200+ products online and 3 shops on Google Maps, with directions
  • Google PageSpeed score of 100 for performance, accessibility and SEO, on mobile and desktop
  • 7 videos ready to post, all sharing the same end screen
ytv_s_learned: Building a brand from scratch is mostly about holding the same choices everywhere, from the logo to the videos. Show options rather than ask for opinions: three versions of the end screen settled in one message a colour question that had dragged on for days. The client's own footage, his rice huller running or his machines at the factory, builds more trust than any stock video.
